claims.text: High-entropy-alloy multilayers with larger individual layer thicknesses tend to form discrete localized shear bands under load.
Reducing individual layer thickness to approximately 10 nm increases the density of amorphous-like interfaces.
At an individual layer thickness of approximately 10 nm, deformation changes from cutting-like shear bands to a kinking-like mode.
The transition to kinking-like deformation produces strain delocalization.
Strain delocalization suppresses time-dependent plastic deformation under sustained loading.
The proposed controlled comparison uses coatings with approximately 10 nm and 40 nm individual layers while holding overall composition and processing conditions constant.
The governing structural mediator is a high density of amorphous/amorphous interfaces in the ultrathin-layer coating.
Increased interface density interrupts the formation of localized shear bands.
Kinking-like deformation spreads strain across multiple layers.
Approximately 10 nm layers will exhibit lower creep strain than approximately 40 nm layers.
Approximately 10 nm layers will deform more uniformly and show less concentrated shear banding than thicker layers.
Approximately 10 nm layers will retain hardness better over prolonged loading than approximately 40 nm layers.
Approximately 40 nm layers will exhibit conventional shear-band-dominated deformation.
Thicker-layer coatings will undergo greater time-dependent plastic deformation under sustained loading.
The mechanism applies only while the multilayer retains an amorphous or near-amorphous interfacial structure and is tested at moderate stress and temperature.
Crystallization or extreme mechanical or thermal conditions may invalidate the proposed mechanism.
The critical layer thickness may vary with alloy composition and processing history.
The hypothesis is falsified if approximately 10 nm coatings show neither reduced creep strain nor a transition away from localized shear banding relative to approximately 40 nm controls.
